title: Have These Reviews Changed?
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/real-deal · Status: working prototype (Chrome, amazon.in)

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
text:
What this project is about
When you shop online, a product’s star average and a few top reviews have to answer two questions:

How sure can I be about that average? 4.4★ from 22 ratings and 4.4★ from 11,000 ratings are not the same evidence.
Does it still describe the product sold today? Products change: a new supplier, a new formula, new packaging. A 4.5★ average built over four years can hide a product that got worse last spring.

Real Deal is a Chrome extension for amazon.in that answers both. It reads the reviews you open, groups their sentences into themes (“battery life”, “missing pieces in the box”), and tests whether each theme’s share of reviews really changed or could just be luck.
Everything runs inside your browser: the language model, the statistics and the storage. The extension makes no network requests, and Chrome enforces that.
What to expect: what the extension shows, the statistics behind each part, how I checked the method on real Amazon data, and what went wrong along the way.

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
text:
How it works

1. How sure is the average?
The product page shows the share of 1★ to 5★ ratings and the number of ratings. From them I rebuild the counts and treat the true star shares as unknown, with a Dirichlet posterior (a Jeffreys prior, α = 0.5 for each star level). Drawing 4,000 samples of the average gives a 90% range: likely 3.8–4.7.
I tried a uniform prior first. On products where almost every rating is 5★, its “90%” range held the true value only 74% of the time in simulation. The Jeffreys prior brought that to 88–91%.


2. What do reviewers talk about?

Reviews are split into sentences. Hinglish and page junk (“The media could not be loaded”) are removed.
Each sentence becomes a vector using all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a 23 MB sentence model that runs in a Web Worker inside the extension.
Spherical k-means groups similar sentences. The number of themes (3 to 8) is chosen by the silhouette score.
c-TF-IDF (the labelling idea from BERTopic) finds each theme’s keywords. If Chrome’s built-in Gemini Nano is available, it turns them into a readable name. The name is kept only if it uses the theme’s own keywords.

A review “mentions” a theme if any of its sentences falls into it. That gives, for each theme and month, k of n reviews mentioned it.


3. Did the theme’s share change?
For every month boundary, the test compares the share before and after with a binomial likelihood ratio and keeps the largest. Searching every month for the biggest difference will always find something. So the p-value comes from a permutation test: shuffle which reviews mention the theme 999 times, redo the whole search each time, and see how often chance alone produces a difference this large.
A product has several themes, so several tests run at once. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false-discovery rate across them. A theme is shown as Real change only if q ≤ 0.10.
The star-filter trap. Amazon shows at most 100 reviews per sort or filter. To reach older reviews, you have to open filters like “1★ only”. But if the later months come mostly from the 1★ filter, every complaint theme seems to “rise”. In those cases the test switches to a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel version that compares 1★ reviews only with 1★ reviews, 5★ only with 5★, and so on.
The Sony example above shows why this matters. “Good sound quality” fell from 62% to 44% of reviews, which looks dramatic. But much of the recent sample came from the 1★ filter. Compared like with like, the drop is no larger than chance would produce, so the verdict is Could just be luck.



Sony headphones (493 reviews over 40 months): large-looking drops that the star-level comparison shows could be luck. The box crosses the 0 line.


What a real change looks like. On the Realme neckband at the top of this post, short verdicts about the product fell from 30% to 12% of reviews after January 2026: −19 points, with a likely range of −31 to −7 that stays well away from 0 (q = 0.04). The typical sentences show what moved: “Not good for calling” before, “Everything is good” after. The test can’t say why: a fix to call quality, or a change in who reviews. It also shows a known weakness. This theme mixes “good” and “not good”, because sentence vectors group by topic more than by opinion.


4. Search results: which rating can you trust?
Sorting by average rating puts 5.0★ from 3 ratings above 4.3★ from 2,000. Instead, each result gets
\[\tilde r = \frac{C\,m + N\,\bar r}{C + N} - 1.645\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{C+N}},\]
a rating pulled towards a typical one, then lowered by its uncertainty. I estimated the constants from the research data: typical rating m = 3.98★, per-review spread σ = 1.34, prior weight C ≈ 5 ratings. So 4.6★ from 9 ratings scores about 3.79, while 4.3★ from 2,000 scores about 4.25. “Sort this page” reorders only the current page. It never loads more.


5. Unusual floods of reviews
The check finds the busiest 14-day window and asks how likely that many reviews would be at the product’s usual pace, using a Poisson tail corrected for having searched every window. It reports a signal only if the burst is very unlikely (p < 0.001) and those reviews were also clearly more positive or more often unverified than the rest.

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
section: Does it work? Checking on real data
text:
Does it work? Checking on real data
I checked the method in a Python notebook on the McAuley Lab Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset (All_Beauty), running the same steps as the extension, with sentence embeddings computed on a laptop GPU.
False alarms and power. In simulation, with a theme at 10% of reviews:



Share of simulated products flagged. The left point (no change) is the false-alarm rate, about 5% at every size. The other points show how often a real change is caught.


The false-alarm rate stays near 5% at every size. With 300 reviews, a rise from 10% to 25% is caught 85% of the time. With 100 reviews, only 43% of the time. So “Could just be luck” with about 100 reviews means “not enough reviews to tell”, not “nothing changed”. The panel says so.
A real product change, found at the right month. Across 50 products with long histories, the test flagged 86 theme changes in 33 products. The clearest was a pack of wipes. A theme about packaging, new, open rose from 8% to 40% of reviews from June 2021 (q = 0.008). I then read the reviews: “They changed the packaging. They no longer use the good snap shut packaging”, and “New packaging awful… Impossible to open!!!”



Reviews of the wipes product mentioning packaging or opening, per half-year, with 95% ranges. (A keyword version of the theme, for illustration.)


Not every detected change is a product change. Reading the other flagged products, I found changes in who buys the product (a spray bottle that went from “curly hair” to “plant misting” reviews), shifts in reviewing culture (incentivized reviews before Amazon’s 2016 ban), and listings that bundle several products. The statistics can say that something changed. Only reading can say what. That’s why every theme in the panel shows its most typical sentences.
A suspicious burst. One eye cream received 109 reviews in 14 days, against a usual pace of about 3. Those reviews averaged 4.81★ against 4.27★, and 99% were unverified against 34%. This is exactly the pattern the Review pattern check looks for. It’s still a signal, not proof.

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
section: What went wrong, and what it taught me
text:
What went wrong, and what it taught me
I logged every problem, why it happened, and why my tests didn’t catch it earlier: 53 entries so far. A few that changed the design:

“Collect everything” isn’t possible. Amazon shows at most 100 reviews per sort or filter. The extension now works through filters, merges them without duplicates, and shows how much of the history it holds (“493 of 7,469 reviews, 40 months”).
Stratifying all the time hid real changes. The star-level test is less powerful, so it now runs only when filtered views were used and the collection is incomplete.
A small language model fails in quiet ways. Gemini Nano sometimes added numbers that weren’t in the results, wrote “over 100” for 87, or turned “fell” into “rose”. Every summary is now checked against the test results: each number must appear there, and no change can be claimed when none is significant. If a check fails, a plain template is used instead.
Statistics people can read. Early versions showed p, q and Δ. Most people can’t use those. The panel now shows a verdict (Real change, Could just be luck, Not proven), a monthly chart and one plain sentence with the counts. The numbers are under “Details”.
Present in the page isn’t the same as visible. The search score badges passed every test but weren’t visible in Chrome: Amazon clips the title link they were placed in. Tests on saved pages can’t see CSS.

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
text:
Is this new?
The building blocks are established, and this project applies them rather than inventing them:

c-TF-IDF topic labels: Grootendorst, BERTopic (2022).
Change-point tests with permutation p-values: a standard non-parametric approach for scanning statistics.
False-discovery rate: Benjamini & Hochberg (1995).
Shrinking ratings with few votes: the Bayesian average used by many ranking systems, here with a lower confidence bound and constants estimated from data.

Existing tools answer different questions. Amazon’s “Customers say” summarises reviews, but has no time dimension and no uncertainty. Fakespot (shut down in 2025) and ReviewMeta graded authenticity on their own servers. Keepa tracks price history, not reviews.
What Real Deal adds is the combination: per-theme change tests over time, with false-discovery control and a fix for Amazon’s star filters, running entirely on-device, and explained in plain language.

title: Have These Reviews Changed?
text:
Limitations and next steps

It sees only the reviews you open, and Amazon decides which 100 reviews each view shows.
About 100 reviews only detect large shifts.
Failures can rise over time as units age, even if the product hasn’t changed.
A theme can merge two related topics.
Hindi and Hinglish reviews are skipped, because the model is English-only.

Next, I’d add a multilingual model for Hindi and Hinglish, split themes that merge two topics, and support Flipkart.
The takeaway: a star average is one number standing in for years of changing experiences. Asking how sure and since when turns it into something you can actually decide with, and both questions can be answered on your own computer.
The formulas, the validation notebook and the full log of decisions are in the GitHub repo.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/promo-optimization-engine · Status: complete

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
What this project is about
Retailers usually judge a promotion by comparing sales during it with a normal week. That number mixes the discount’s real effect with everything else happening at the same time.
This project separates them. It measures how many extra sales a discount actually causes, uses that to plan which product gets which discount in which week, checks the result with a second model, and asks whether a store test could prove it.
What to expect: a simple example of why promo sales mislead, how each step works, the results, and how much they can be trusted.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
One discount, four stories
A box of cereal goes 20% off and sales double, from 100 boxes to 200. Success?
Maybe not. That week the cereal was probably also on the front of the flyer and on an end-of-aisle display. Some of those 200 boxes would have sold anyway, now at a lower price. And some shoppers simply switched from the cereal next to it.
All four stories are hidden inside “sales doubled”. Plan from that number, and you keep paying for discounts that don’t earn their cost.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
How it works
Data. dunnhumby’s The Complete Journey: two years of grocery shopping by about 2,500 households, with flyer and display records. I used the 137 top-selling products over 99 weeks.
Measuring the real effect. I asked: in weeks when the discount was deeper than usual, beyond what the flyer, display, season and recent sales would explain, did sales rise more than expected? That’s the idea behind Double ML: remove everything else first, so the discount only gets credit for what’s left. A placebo test with shuffled discounts checks that the method doesn’t invent effects.
Planning the calendar. Over 8 weeks with 10 promo slots a week, each product can get 10%, 20% or 30% off, or nothing, under a budget, a cap per category and no back-to-back weeks. Because these rules interact, I used an integer program solved with OR-Tools CP-SAT, and compared it with a common rule of thumb: deepest discount on the best sellers.
Checking from the top down. A Bayesian marketing mix model (PyMC-Marketing) of weekly sales for 8 whole categories, with discount, flyer and display as levers, allowing for lingering effects and diminishing returns.
Designing the test. Run the new calendar in half the stores and compare weekly promo margin, using CUPED (adjusting for each store’s pre-test sales) to cut noise. I simulated it 1,000 times on real store history.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
Results









Effect (θ)
What 10% off does




Naive: promo weeks vs. normal weeks
3.49
+42% units


Double ML: other factors removed
2.51 (95% CI 2.18–2.85)
+29% units


Placebo: discounts shuffled
0.01
nothing, as it should



The naive view overstates the discount by about 40%, because it gives the discount credit for the flyer and display. And 44% of promo-week sales would have happened anyway.
Planning pays. Same rules, same $5k budget:




Extra margin
Budget used




“Deepest discount on top sellers”
$60
all of it


Optimised calendar
$719
37% less



The rule of thumb loses because 30% off only pays for itself on about 1 in 4 products. On the rest, the discount given on sales that would have happened anyway outweighs the extra sales.



Margin returned per $1 of retailer discount, by category (94% credible intervals).


Most discounts don’t pay for themselves. In 7 of 8 categories, each $1 of discount brings back less than $1 of margin. Soft drinks return about $0.69, and only frozen pizza clears break-even.
A surprise. Both models rank the categories the same way, but the category-level effect is only about half the product-level one. That’s cannibalisation: when one cereal is discounted, part of its jump is taken from the cereal next to it. So the $719 above is probably about twice too high. The comparison still holds, since both plans use the same estimates, but the dollar figure is optimistic.
Could a test prove it?



Chance that an 8-week test detects a given true lift, with and without CUPED.


The test is fair (about 5% false alarms with no real change), but with 84 usable stores it reliably detects only lifts of 13% or more. The calendar is expected to add about 3%, which it would catch only about 10% of the time, even with CUPED tripling its power. So a “not significant” result wouldn’t mean the calendar failed. Proving 3% would need about 1,500 stores.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
Is this new?
No, not as an idea. Each piece is well established, and this project applies them rather than inventing them:

Double ML: Chernozhukov et al., Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters (The Econometrics Journal, 2018).
Where the promo bump comes from: van Heerde, Leeflang & Wittink, Decomposing the Sales Promotion Bump with Store Data (Marketing Science, 2004). They found that, on average, about a third of the bump comes from shoppers switching brands.
Promo planning as an integer program: Cohen et al., The Impact of Linear Optimization on Promotion Planning (Operations Research, 2017). They estimated a potential profit gain of about 3%, close to the gain my optimiser predicts.
Marketing mix models with carryover and diminishing returns: Google, Bayesian Methods for Media Mix Modeling with Carryover and Shape Effects (2017).
CUPED: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (WSDM 2013).

What this project adds is small and practical: it connects the four steps on one public dataset, uses a second model to catch the first one’s overstatement, and checks before running a test whether that test could detect the predicted gain.

title: Almost Half of Promo Sales Would Have Happened Anyway
text:
Limitations and next steps
The data is observational, so the Double ML result holds only if I’ve measured what drives both promo decisions and sales. There’s no cost data: margin (30% of price), supplier funding (50% of the discount) and display costs are assumptions. Cannibalisation and stock-piling are handled with simple rules, and the 2,500-household panel makes the test far weaker than a real retailer’s full store sales would. Next, I’d scale product-level effects to category level before optimising, model stock-piling directly, and compare other test designs, such as alternating weeks.
The takeaway: judge a promotion by the sales it creates, not the sales it records. Almost half of promo volume was going to happen anyway.
Full code, results and every number above are in the GitHub repo.

title: Samina Yasmin
text:
Hi, I’m Samina. I’m curious about why people pick what they pick, and why models do too.
I started out at IIT Madras, modelling how people behave at work. Now I study how models behave with data. Turns out they’re not so different: both are confident, and both are sometimes wrong.
Here I take things apart to see how they really work, and share what I find.

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/transaction-risk-decision-framework · Status: in progress

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
What this project is about
Banks score every card transaction for fraud risk. But a score doesn’t stop fraud by itself. Someone still has to decide: approve the payment, send it to an analyst to review, or decline it.
This project builds that decision step. It combines the fraud probability, the transaction amount and the cost of each possible mistake, then picks the cheapest action for each transaction, without exceeding the number of reviews analysts can handle.
What to expect: a simple example of why a score isn’t enough, how each action is priced, four ways of deciding compared on unseen data, and how much we can trust the result.

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
section: How this differs from my IIT Madras project
text:
How this differs from my IIT Madras project
I first worked on this problem in a coursework project at IIT Madras: Credit Default and Fraud Risk Prediction (American Express – IIT Madras, 2022). I cleaned the data, balanced the classes with SMOTE-Tomek, and compared seven models. XGBoost did best on ROC-AUC and F1.
That project asked “how risky is this case?” This one asks what a risk team needs next: “what do we do about it, and what will it cost?”









IIT Madras coursework
This project




Output
A risk score
Approve, review or decline


Rare fraud cases
Oversampled
Left as they are, so probabilities stay realistic


Testing
Random splits
Train on the past, test on a later period


Judged by
ROC-AUC, F1
€ cost, fraud caught, customers affected

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
Two transactions, same score
A €3 coffee and a €900 laptop both get a 10% fraud score. The common rule, “decline if the score is above 0.5”, approves both.
But if the laptop is fraud, the bank loses €900 plus fees. An analyst check costs about €5, which is clearly worth it for the laptop and not for the coffee. Same score, different right answer.

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
How it works
Data. The public ULB credit-card dataset: 284,807 European card transactions over two days, 492 of them fraud (0.17%).
Model. LightGBM, trained on the first 60% of the timeline and tested on the last 20%, as it would be used in real life. Unlike my coursework project, I didn’t oversample fraud. Oversampling inflates the scores, so a “10%” stops meaning 10%. Here the probability feeds a € calculation, so it has to be honest.
Pricing each action. With p = fraud probability and A = amount:
approve = p × (A + fees)
review  = analyst cost + p × (share analysts miss) × (A + fees) + (1 − p) × customer delay
decline = (1 − p) × (lost margin + cost of an annoyed customer)
For the laptop: €92 to approve, €15 to review, €33 to decline, so it goes to review. For the coffee: €1.80 to approve, so it goes through. The cost inputs (€5 per review, 90% of fraud caught on review, and so on) are assumptions that a real bank’s Finance team would supply.
Four ways of deciding:

P0: approve everything (the cost of doing nothing)
P1: decline if p > 0.5 (the common default)
P2: two cut-offs, tuned on past data
P3: the cheapest action per transaction, within a review cap of 1%

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
Results



Total cost per 1,000 test transactions. Black lines show the 95% range.






P1: decline if p > 0.5
P3: cheapest action




Cost per 1,000 transactions
€89.8
€69.4


Share of fraud € stopped
49%
68%


Analyst reviews used
0
33 (of 569 allowed)



P3 wins by doing exactly what the laptop example suggests: it spends a few reviews on risky, expensive transactions that the 0.5 rule lets through.
How sure are we? The test period has only 75 frauds, so I resampled it 1,000 times. P3 beats approving everything in 99.7% of resamples, and beats the 0.5 rule in 85%. The second gain is promising but not proven: its 95% range is −€352 to €3,493. I’d use it to justify a pilot, not to promise savings.
A surprise. P2, the tuned cut-offs, did slightly worse than the plain 0.5 rule. It was tuned on just 33 frauds, so it mostly fitted noise. P3 has nothing to tune, which helps when fraud examples are scarce.
If analysts cost more? Raising the review cost from €1 to €20, P3 uses fewer reviews (133 down to 4), and its cost stays around €67–70 per 1,000, against €90 for the 0.5 rule.

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
Is this new?
No, not as an idea. Making decisions by expected cost is well established, and this project applies it rather than inventing it:

Cost-based thresholds: Elkan, The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning (IJCAI 2001).
Cost-based fraud decisions, per transaction: Correa Bahnsen et al., Cost Sensitive Credit Card Fraud Detection Using Bayes Minimum Risk (ICMLA 2013), and their later work on example-dependent costs.
A “review” option beside yes/no: the reject option, formalised by Chow (1957, 1970).
Resampling distorts probabilities: Dal Pozzolo et al., Calibrating Probability with Undersampling for Unbalanced Classification (IEEE SSCI 2015). This is from the same ULB group that released the dataset.
Limited analyst capacity in fraud: Dal Pozzolo et al., Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy (IEEE TNNLS 2018).

What this project adds is small and practical: it puts these pieces into one end-to-end pipeline, with three actions, amount-based costs, a review cap and a test on a later time period. It also reports how uncertain the gain is, which most public work on this dataset skips, and shows that tuned cut-offs can fail when fraud examples are few.

title: Same Fraud Score, Different Decision
text:
Limitations and next steps
The costs are assumptions, there are few frauds, and the data covers only two days with no customer IDs. Next, I’d move the same decision layer to the larger IEEE-CIS dataset, keep each customer in only one of training or testing, and simulate chargebacks arriving weeks later, as they do in practice.
The takeaway: a fraud model’s job is to estimate risk. Deciding what to do with that risk is a separate job, and it’s where most of the money is.
Full details, formulas and a one-page decision memo are in the GitHub repo.
